04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The archivist's second response provided an instructive test of Emma's discipline. Three October 2011 subject-index entries appeared to concern the Glenarraidh Education Trust's travel scheme, one of them the item dated 12 October and labelled “decision not received”. The archive could release their dates and general classifications, not the original correspondence or identifying details. It also cautioned that the surviving index might be incomplete.

The other two headings referred broadly to selection questions and an information request. Emma transcribed them without attempting to reconstruct the letters underneath. The classifications had been supplied by newspaper staff: they were editorial descriptions, not authenticated statements from the people who had written in.

“Three complainants,” Sarah announced over the telephone.

“Three entries,” Emma corrected. “Not necessarily three authors, still less three established grievances. We can't even assume the index captured every letter.”

She annotated each record with the limits of its provenance. A shared subject did not prove common authorship, nor did a repeated label establish that any recipient had failed to receive a decision notice. She was wary of manufacturing a pattern merely by placing fragments side by side.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived later that day. The trust had still found no completed contact-attempt forms. Another page of the office guidance directed staff to document correspondence returned as undeliverable, but Fiona could not confirm consistent compliance. The appeals folder remained unopened. Emma recorded the procedural expectation separately from any claim about what had happened in practice.

The documentary trail was becoming more detailed without becoming conclusive. A model letter demonstrated intended notification; a dispatch ledger could contain entries marked as sent; a returned-post policy explained a response to one kind of failed delivery. None by itself established receipt or comprehension. And the ability to seek reconsideration within fourteen days of receiving a decision was not identical to merely being sent the relevant information.

Emma reopened the notes she had made during her 18 September 2011 interview with Claire. The teacher had questioned the difference between what the trust promised and what students received. Emma had once treated her unease as resentment towards its management, a reading that had suited a hurried newspaper story. Recognising that error now offered no retrospective proof of wrongdoing. It did, however, make the temptation to compress uncertainty into a dramatic account particularly uncomfortable.

She revised the labels in her notebook: Prepared, Dispatched, Received, Understood. These were successive propositions requiring different evidence. The archive's three entries might eventually illuminate one of them, but their wording did not yet do so.

Sarah asked whether Emma intended to publish. She could envisage a carefully qualified account of the procedures documented by the trust and the limits of their surviving records. She could not responsibly allege that particular students had been deprived of a review, or that the foundation had deliberately withheld decisions.

Before answering, she noticed a subtlety in the archivist's email. The three entries were drawn from different sections of the index, whose categories had not been explained. Emma had treated their common subject as grounds for comparison; the archive's internal arrangement might instead reflect different types of correspondence or different cataloguing practices.

She sent a final, narrowly framed question: how had those sections been organised in 2011, and were their headings intended to identify the writers' concerns or merely facilitate filing?

Emma closed her notebook with an uncomfortable but necessary recognition: assembling more clues did not remove the obligation to understand what each clue actually was.
